claims.text: A eutectic high-entropy alloy can possess a fine lamellar microstructure consisting of alternating soft FCC and hard B2 phases.
The alloy initially has an intact passivating surface oxide typical of high-temperature environments.
Accelerated coupled wear-corrosion degradation is driven by synergistic interactions at FCC/B2 phase boundaries.
Mechanical wear preferentially removes or damages the passive film on the softer, more corrosion-prone FCC phase.
Wear-induced exposure of chemically distinct phases establishes micro-galvanic cells between them.
Micro-galvanic coupling accelerates localized corrosion at exposed interphase regions.
Localized corrosion weakens interphase bonding and thereby increases subsequent wear.
The mutual enhancement of corrosion and wear creates a self-amplifying degradation cycle.
At around 700°C or higher, passivation in the proposed alloy is marginal or compromised.
A corrosive medium with sufficient ionic species is required to drive the proposed galvanic reactions.
The mechanical load must continuously disrupt the surface film for substantial wear-corrosion synergy to occur.
Combined material loss under simultaneous wear and corrosion will exceed the loss under either isolated wear or isolated corrosion.
The wear rate under coupled exposure will be greater than the wear rate measured under isolated wear.
The corrosion rate under coupled exposure will be greater than the corrosion rate measured under isolated corrosion.
Total degradation under coupled exposure will be greater than the additive sum of independently measured wear and corrosion damage.
A homogenized single-phase microstructure will not support extensive phase-to-phase galvanic coupling.
